lessons.title: My arts choices this term
lessons.outcome: Add a review to my arts log.
lessons.goal: I can use my real work to say what I tried and learned.
success: I can choose real work from this term.
I can say what I tried and what changed.
I can start a review in my own words.
words: Look back and say what you think.
Something you did in a new way.
A record of your arts work.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your art, tests and arts log.
Choose two real pieces or notes from this term.
You may review with just an adult.
stages.say: Bring the actual work from Weeks 1 to 5 and the log. The pupil chooses two useful examples, such as a colour or sound response and the later changed piece. A precise witnessed sound or movement record is valid. If an item is missing, mark the gap honestly. We are looking at the pupil’s arts choices, not asking for a personal life story.
stages.good: The pupil identifies actual work, or an honest current record. No earlier artefact is invented and private review is available.
stages.fallback: Read a real earlier witness note aloud. If none exists, invite a short current oral account and label it as recollection today. It does not prove a missing earlier performance.
stages.answer: An original work, actual log or precise earlier witness note can support a claim. A new recollection is labelled as recollection.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Look or listen: what did you make?
Star: what part worked for your idea?
Tool: what did you change or learn?
stages.say: Use the eye and ear, numbered stars and tool picture prompts. The pupil may point while you read the labels. The stars prompt specific helpful features, not scores. Model the frames: I made ___. I chose ___ because ___. I changed ___. Keep the picture strip visible beside the pupil’s own work.
stages.good: The pupil links a prompt to a real feature and begins to distinguish a choice from a general judgement.
stages.fallback: Say the short labels look, listen, helpful part and change. Use gestures or spoken choices if printed prompts cannot be seen.
stages.answer: A useful comment names a real feature, such as a soft beat or wide gap. Nice alone does not tell us what the pupil noticed.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch a short review of an adult example.
The adult points to a real feature.
Hear one reason and one thing learned.
stages.say: Make a tiny adult silent sequence with a short pause, then repeat it with a longer pause. Say: I made a quiet sequence. I chose a slow ending for my calm idea. I changed the pause so the ending was easier for me to notice. I learned to test a change. Date it today. Explain that this is an adult example made now, not a pupil’s half-term evidence. Model a short accurate scribed sentence and read it back.
stages.good: The model connects a real action, a choice, a change and learning. The record uses the maker’s words and identifies the real date.
stages.fallback: Perform or direct the two silent versions. The pupil can listen to an exact description and confirm the difference without moving.
stages.answer: Check: Which tells us more, it was good or I made the pause longer? The second identifies an actual change. Ask what changed in the model.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help review the adult example.
Choose the sentence that fits the work.
Keep a fact about the work and a personal view apart.
stages.say: Read two options: A I made every piece perfectly; B I made the pause longer and liked the clearer ending. Ask which the actual model supports. Choose B. Build one short review together, then leave the pupil’s own review open. Read back any scribed words. Do not turn the class model into an answer the pupil must copy.
stages.good: The pupil selects a statement supported by the actual work and can add or confirm their own view.
stages.fallback: Offer the two statements orally and accept a point, sign or agreed yes or no signal. Repeat the actual pause if needed.
stages.answer: If A is chosen, show the one change again. Parallel check: Can one silent sequence prove every piece was perfect? No. Use one observed feature instead.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, choose your two examples.
I made ___. I chose ___ because ___.
One part I changed was ___.
I learned ___. I want to try ___.
stages.say: Spend about eight minutes on the pupil’s review of the chosen examples. Use the picture prompts and one sentence starter at a time. Accept two or three meaningful sentences, recorded signs, drawings with the pupil’s explanation or exact scribed words. Then spend about six minutes looking across grid rows 1 to 3. Locate real evidence and add a brief comment or mark more to do or not yet seen. Use existing evidence rather than remaking all weeks. The pupil owns the review; the adult may write a separately labelled observation.
stages.good: The review refers to actual work and a real choice or change. Grid rows have honest evidence references or gaps. Pupil and adult comments remain distinct.
stages.fallback: Use oral review and real witness notes. An adult records the pupil’s confirmed words when recording materials become available. Keep the actual date and do not claim a written entry exists until recorded.
stages.answer: Possible pupil wording: I used a soft sound. I changed the last pause. I learned to try my idea twice. Accept different wording when the work supports it.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Hear your words read back.
Change any words that do not sound like you.
Keep the real work with your review.
stages.say: Read the review aloud privately. Ask if it says what the pupil meant. Let them correct a word, point to different evidence or say that a memory is uncertain. Use the last two minutes to store the work and log together. Mark which rows still need a conversation next lesson.
stages.good: The pupil confirms or corrects their own review. Evidence is stored and gaps remain visible without a penalty or invented success.
stages.fallback: Repeat the oral review in short parts, allowing an agreed signal to confirm or change each part.
stages.answer: The pupil can change a scribe’s wording. Support does not remove ownership, but the record must name the help used.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My review says ___.
One thing I learned was ___.
Next time I will finish my review.
stages.say: Date this draft review and record the form and support used. Keep the pupil’s chosen evidence references and the first grid comments. This is a draft for Tuesday, not a completed award claim.
stages.good: An honest dated review draft and evidence trail are ready for the second lesson.
stages.fallback: Retain a precise oral or signed review note at the next recording opportunity. Label a pending record honestly.
stages.answer: A short review can be sufficient when it captures the pupil’s own choices, learning and evidence. Length is not the assessment target.

Supported: Choose two real examples with an adult.
Use one picture and sentence start at a time.
Say or show a choice and a change.
Hear your words back and check the first grid rows.
Independent: Choose two examples from this term.
Write what you chose, changed and learned.
Point to the evidence for your review.
Check grid rows 1 to 3 with an adult.
Aspire: Review two examples in your own words.
Explain a change with a before and after feature.
Say how a test helped your learning.
Name one next step and check the grid.

log: My real examples and dates are ___.
I made ___. I chose ___ because ___.
One part I changed was ___.
I learned ___. Next I want to try ___.
My words were scribed: yes / no. I checked them: yes / not yet.
demo: Choose actual work or a real witness note.
Say one choice or change and its reason.
Read the review back and match it to evidence.
models: Adult example made today: I made a silent sequence. I changed the pause. The ending was clearer to me. I learned to test one change.

hinge.question: Which review fits the real adult example?

options.B: I changed the pause and liked the clearer ending.

hinge.feedback: B names a real change and a personal view.
hinge.wrong_feedback: Look at the one real change. It cannot prove that every piece was perfect.

half_term_outcomes: Use colour/sound to express a feeling.
Create art linked to an emotion (links PSHE).
Find out about an artist who expresses feelings.
Try a new expressive technique.
Review and improve my piece.
Add a review to my arts log.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Show one prompt at a time. Model a short example, then fade to a sentence start. Revisit the same words and use the actual work beside the prompt. Chunk the six-week grid into two groups of three. Allow thinking time.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Read all prompts aloud. Accept pointing, signing, speaking, drawing or pupil-directed adult recording. Offer a choice before an open question. Read scribed words back and let the pupil correct them.
adaptations.semh: Keep review private and about choices in the work. Use invented or abstract ideas and avoid questions about personal adversity. No grades, rankings or public performance. Offer a calm pause and an agreed return cue.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Offer a seated, silent route and a large print view. Use a description or precise witnessed sequence where a visual piece is inaccessible. The pupil can direct adult handling. Keep actual support visible in the record.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Read the source note or prompt slowly and check meaning. Accept oral ideas before writing. Translate with support where available while retaining the pupil’s intended meaning.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Artists use reviews and research to make choices and explain their work. These habits also support clear communication in many kinds of work.

kit: Actual arts log and own work from Weeks 1 to 5, including the Week 3 plan where relevant.
Six-outcome evidence sheet; keep actual dates, locations, pupil words and support.
Book and ordinary writing tools if available; oral or signed responses and adult scribing are valid.
Picture prompt strip from the accepted pack, read with its labels. No new art materials are needed.

cover.catch_up: Use the actual available evidence. Date any new review or research today. Mark unavailable earlier work as a gap and never reconstruct it as old evidence.
cover.stop_rule: Pause the task, lower the demand and offer the agreed quiet space. Return with one short prompt. No personal disclosure or public display is required.

ta_focus.I do: Point to the evidence or source. Read the short frame and check meaning.
ta_focus.We do: Offer a brief question or choice, then wait. Model only the first step if needed.
ta_focus.Create: Scribe the pupil’s own words, read them back and record the real support. Keep adult judgement separate.

lessons.evidence: Keep the pupil’s dated own-word review or research, actual source or work reference, accurate support and the six-outcome tick-and-comment grid. Mark missing or unfinished evidence honestly. No completed award is inferred.

cold_call.foundation: Point to the source or piece you used.
cold_call.middle: What does this feature tell you?
cold_call.higher: Which evidence supports your view, and what remains uncertain?

misconceptions: An adult scribe means it is not my review.
The ideas remain yours when the adult records your words, reads them back and notes the help.
A tick means the whole award is complete.
The grid records these six weekly outcomes only. Wider requirements and genuine evidence need a separate judgement.
A good review says everything was perfect.
Name a real strength, change or learning point and an achievable next step.
slide_titles: I do and your arts log
We do and your arts log
comparison: Too vague
My art was good.
Ask which real feature the maker means.
A useful review
I made the pause longer. The ending was clearer to me.
This adult example links a real change to the maker’s view. Use your own details.

lessons.title: My finished arts review
lessons.outcome: Add a review to my arts log.
lessons.goal: I can add my own checked review to my arts log.
success: I can say what I tried and learned.
I can check my review against real work.
I can keep my review and one next step.
words: Look back and say what you think.
Something you did in a new way.
A record of your arts work.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your review and real examples.
Read or hear your own words again.
Choose one part to check today.
stages.say: Recover Monday’s review, the actual pieces or witness notes and the six-outcome grid. If absent last time, use an honest review of the available work today. Keep missing earlier evidence marked as a gap. Do not let the pupil’s review become a test of memory.
stages.good: The pupil identifies a real review starting point and a manageable task.
stages.fallback: Read actual prior notes or use today’s labelled recollection. Give time to confirm or correct the account.
stages.answer: A review written today must use today’s date. Earlier work keeps its original date where known.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Picture prompts help you tell the story of your work.
What did you try? What changed?
What will you try next?
stages.say: Revisit the eye or ear, stars and tool. Ask the pupil to choose the most useful prompt for their review. A next step is a small action, such as trying a different gap or practising a pause. It is not a promise to be perfect.
stages.good: The pupil chooses a prompt and identifies a possible small next action.
stages.fallback: Read the prompt labels aloud and accept a spoken or gestured choice.
stages.answer: A feasible next step names something to do. Try a softer start is clearer than be the best.

stages.name: I do
pupil: See how the adult checks a review.
Does the work show the change?
The maker can correct the scribed words.
stages.say: Use yesterday’s adult model or make and date a fresh one. Read: I made the pause longer. Compare the actual versions. Then deliberately read a mistaken scribe sentence: I made every sound louder. Ask the maker to correct it. Replace it with the confirmed wording. Model a final next step and show how one grid row links to the real dated example, while an unseen row stays not yet seen.
stages.good: The adult demonstrates checking, correction and honest evidence selection without completing pupil rows for them.
stages.fallback: Use a real short silent demonstration and oral comparison. Give an agreed signal to stop the read-back at an inaccurate word.
stages.answer: Check: Who owns the review, the adult who writes or the pupil whose ideas it records? The pupil. Ask them to correct the example.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help match a comment to the real example.
Choose shown, more to do or not yet seen.
A tick needs a real comment or record.
stages.say: Use the adult example and a practice grid row outside the pupil grid. Hinge: We cannot find any earlier record. Should we A tick shown anyway, or B mark not yet seen and say what is missing? Choose B. Distinguish a gap from a failure. A pupil may have taken part even when a record is unavailable. Do not assume either completion or non-participation.
stages.good: The pupil recognises that honest assessment uses actual evidence and can leave an outcome unconfirmed.
stages.fallback: Give the two choices orally. Use a spoken status and scribed comment if ticks are inaccessible.
stages.answer: If A is chosen, ask a parallel check: Can a blank folder show the change we want to review? No. We can make a truthful note and choose a next step.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Finish your own review in your book or arts log.
I tried ___. I learned ___.
A change I made was ___. Next I will ___.
Check all six rows with an adult.
stages.say: Use about seven minutes to complete and check the pupil’s review. It may be short, scribed, signed or drawn with an explanation. Use the remaining seven minutes to revisit rows 1 to 3 and review rows 4 to 6. For each outcome, choose one status and add a specific evidence location, date and short comment. Row 6 refers to this actual review. Retain support and pupil words. Keep one next step achievable. Do not manufacture missing earlier work or assess every practical skill again in fourteen minutes.
stages.good: A dated pupil-owned review is added to the log. All six verbatim outcomes have an honest status and comment, including gaps. No adult model substitutes for pupil evidence.
stages.fallback: Conduct the review orally with real records and the pupil’s chosen words. An adult transcribes and reads back at the next opportunity; until then mark the written log as pending.
stages.answer: A valid entry can be: I used colour for a calm idea. I changed a gap after my review. I learned to test a choice. Next I will try a bigger shape. The pupil must supply their own true details.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Hear or read your final review.
Check one strength and your next step.
Keep the review and evidence together.
stages.say: Invite a private share with the supporting adult. Check that the words belong to the pupil and that the evidence matches. A public display is not needed. Record actual support and any unfinished item. Use the final two minutes to tidy and store the log.
stages.good: The pupil confirms the review and can identify its evidence and next step using their preferred response mode.
stages.fallback: Use a private oral or signed review, with adult read-back of any record.
stages.answer: The assessment is of what the evidence shows and what the pupil can explain. Handwriting, speech volume and public confidence are not arts success criteria.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My review is in ___.
I am pleased with ___ because ___.
My next arts step is ___.
stages.say: Record the real location of the review and the pupil’s next step. Confirm that the six-week grid has comments rather than automatic ticks. Spring 1 is complete as a teaching sequence; this does not certify an award or fill an evidence gap.
stages.good: The pupil and adult can find the final review and understand one next step.
stages.fallback: Record the location and confirmed next step in a precise witness note, marking any transcription still pending.
stages.answer: Completed teaching, completed evidence and an award decision are different. Keep each statement true.

Point, sign or say one correction and next step.
Let an adult scribe your own words.
Independent: Check your draft against your work.
Finish the review and one next step.
Complete the six-row review with an adult.

Use real evidence for your view.
Choose a next step that follows your learning.
Help check all six outcomes honestly.

lessons.title: An artist I want to learn about
lessons.outcome: Research an artist or performer who inspires me (Bronze).
lessons.goal: I can research one artist and record checked facts in my own words.
success: I can choose an artist and a question.
I can record facts about their career and work.
I can name my source and explain my interest.
words: Find out about a question using a source.
Where a fact or account comes from.
The work a person does over time.
Give someone an idea or reason to try.
What someone thinks or feels about the work.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your arts log and this term’s work.
Choose a quiet way to read or hear the fact notes.
This research goes in your Explore log.
stages.say: Explain that the scheme names Bronze in this week’s outcome. The current pathway remains Explore. Everyone completes an accessible research record now; the record can also be retained as evidence for later arts inspiration work. It does not automatically complete that level. Bring the actual half-term log and six-outcome grid. No pupil needs an account, phone, internet search or public performance.
stages.good: Pupils understand the core research task and have a private accessible route. The exact scheme outcome is visible without relabelling the whole term.
stages.fallback: Read the supplied fact notes aloud. The pupil may choose, ask and respond orally while an adult records exact confirmed words.
stages.answer: Research is this week’s task for GROW. Only extra depth is optional. The current award level stays Explore.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Read or hear notes M1 and T1.
Choose Henri Matisse or Alma Thomas.
What do you want to find out?
stages.say: Read the short original fact notes. Both artists have long-established public careers. Invite a genuine choice based on a method, career change or idea that interests the pupil. They choose one artist for the record. Another long-established public artist or performer is valid only with an adult-checked factual source and the same record fields. If neither supplied artist inspires them yet, let them research the more interesting method and record an honest response rather than inventing admiration.
stages.good: The pupil chooses one subject and a question, such as how the artist changed a method or found ideas. A reason can be tentative and truthful.
stages.fallback: Offer the two names with a brief spoken description and let the pupil point, sign or say a choice.
stages.answer: Both choices are valid. The pupil’s reason must be their own. Do not score one artist as better than another.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch how the adult reads one fact.
Hide the note. Say its meaning in new words.
Check the fact and name the source.
stages.say: Model with M1: read the account of cut shapes and movable arrangements. Cover it and say, in fresh wording, that Matisse could try new positions for pieces before fixing them. Reopen the note and check the meaning. Name M1 and its printed title. Then say a personal view separately: I like the chance to test a layout. Show that swapping just one word is too close to copying. Write no quotation and reproduce no artwork. Model one career fact and one method fact as different kinds of finding.
stages.good: The adult demonstrates read, cover, explain, check and source. A fact and a personal response remain distinct.
stages.fallback: Read a single fact aloud, pause, ask the pupil to explain it, then read the source again to check meaning. A scribe records the pupil’s wording.
stages.answer: Check: Matisse cut painted paper is a source-supported fact. I find movable shapes useful is a personal view. Either needs accurate labelling.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Sort a fact from a personal view.
Help make a short own-word note.
Keep the source label with the fact.
stages.say: Use T1. Compare A Alma Thomas continued developing her painting after retiring from teaching and B Her repeated marks give me an idea for my piece. Ask which is a checkable fact. Choose A; B is a personal response. Build a new sentence together and check it against the note. Hinge: is changing one word in a copied sentence enough to make the research your own? No. Explain the meaning without looking, then check accuracy. Adult model sentences remain examples, not pupil evidence.
stages.good: The pupil separates fact from response and understands a repeatable own-word research process.
stages.fallback: Use spoken A and B choices and accept a signal. Scribe the pupil’s explanation and read it back.
stages.answer: If B is chosen as fact, ask: Can the source prove what gives you an idea? No. Parallel check: retired in 1960 is a fact; I like this method is a view.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Choose one artist and one research question.
In your log, record a career fact and a work fact.
Use your own words. Keep the source label.
Say why a method or feature interests you.
stages.say: Use about ten minutes for the research record. Read or hear the chosen note, cover it, express the meaning, check it and name the source. Keep one checked career fact and at least one fact about the work or method. Add the pupil’s own response to a specific feature and one remaining question. Pupils may scribe or dictate. Use the last four minutes to locate evidence for grid rows 1 to 3 and mark honest gaps. The supplied note is an access source, not the pupil’s completed research. Do not require copying its sentences.
stages.good: A dated record identifies one artist, a question, at least two accurate own-word findings, a source and a personal reason. Earlier grid rows have evidence comments or gaps.
stages.fallback: Read the note aloud in small parts. The pupil gives an oral or signed response. Scribe exact confirmed wording when possible and mark any later transcription as pending.
stages.answer: Accept, for example, a correctly rephrased career change and one technique detail. If the pupil repeats the note exactly, cover it and ask them to explain the idea to an adult.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Check facts against your chosen note.
Which words are your own view?
Keep one question for Wednesday.
stages.say: Ask the pupil to point to the source for each fact and to identify their personal response. Correct an error together without replacing the pupil’s voice. Note one question or feature to consider next time. Use the final two minutes to store the source prompt, research record and actual log evidence.
stages.good: Facts are checked and separate from interpretation. A genuine question supports the second lesson.
stages.fallback: Read the fact and source aloud and ask for confirmation or correction through the pupil’s chosen response mode.
stages.answer: We can check a method from the source. We cannot infer an artist’s private feelings from the method or impose a universal meaning on a colour.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: I researched ___ because ___.
One fact I checked was ___.
My source was ___. My next question is ___.
stages.say: Date the actual research and record the source label, supplied title, access method and support. Keep the pupil’s own words. Carry the same chosen artist into Wednesday unless the pupil has a clear reason to change. A change of artist needs a real new record, not a relabelled old one.
stages.good: The research has a truthful evidence trail and a clear next step.
stages.fallback: An adult keeps a precise dated note of the pupil’s own oral or signed research and reads it back.
stages.answer: The source can be a supplied printed note read aloud. The log must accurately name that route rather than claim the pupil visited a museum or website.

Ask one question with an adult.
Say a career fact and a work fact in your own words.
Name the note and say what interests you.
Independent: Choose one artist and a question.
Read, cover, explain and check two facts.
Record the source and your personal reason.
Keep one question and check early grid rows.
Aspire: Explain a link between career and method.
Separate checked facts from your interpretation.
Add a question the supplied note does not answer.

demo: Choose one artist and a question.
Read or hear the source note. Pick a career fact and a work fact.
Cover the note. Explain the meaning in your own words.
Check accuracy, name the source and add your own response.
models: Adult example only: Matisse could test where to place cut shapes. That method interests me because I can try a layout before fixing it. Source M1 supports the fact; the reason is my own.

hinge.question: Which is a checkable fact from T1?

options.A: Thomas continued developing painting after retiring from teaching.
options.B: Her repeated marks give me an idea.

hinge.feedback: A is supported by the source. B is a personal response.
hinge.wrong_feedback: B says what gives the maker an idea. Check T1 for the career fact in A.

half_term_outcomes: Explore how artists express resilience and change.
Develop a skill and record it in my arts log.
Plan an artwork on the theme of resilience.
Create my resilience-themed piece.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your research note and the source.
Keep the same chosen artist if it still fits.
Read your question and facts again.
stages.say: Recover Monday’s record and the chosen source note. If missing, create a short honest research record now using the supplied source, dated today. Do not invent a previous visit, interview or study session. Reconfirm that the current log is Explore and the exact scheme outcome names Bronze for progression.
stages.good: The pupil has a real starting record and source, or an honest current catch-up record.
stages.fallback: Read the source and actual research aloud. Accept signed or oral responses with accurate adult scribing.
stages.answer: A record made today is valid when dated today. It does not prove a missing Monday activity.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Which fact did you check?
What feature interests you?
What is still a question?
stages.say: Revisit the pupil’s question. Let them identify what the note answers and what remains unknown. If it does not answer a question, say so. Help narrow the research to the artist’s career and work. Do not invent an answer about private feelings, intentions or events.
stages.good: The pupil can identify a source-supported finding and a remaining uncertainty.
stages.fallback: Offer one fact and one unanswered question orally. The pupil chooses the one supported by the note.
stages.answer: The supplied notes explain public career or method facts. They do not answer every question about the artist.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Hear a fact and a personal reason.
See how an artist’s method can lead to a new idea.
The research uses words, not copied art.
stages.say: Model with T1: Thomas used repeated coloured marks in later abstract painting. My response is that changing the gaps between my own marks could suggest a fresh start. That is my idea, not a reproduction or a claim about Thomas’s feelings. Show how to record source T1, the fact, the specific feature, my reason and a possible next action. Briefly tell the adult listener what I found and note that real private sharing. This is a model only.
stages.good: The model joins accurate research to a personal reason and an original next idea, without copying a work.
stages.fallback: Describe an original pattern of short and long pauses as a possible personal response. The pupil need only explain an idea today; a new finished artwork is not required.
stages.answer: Check: Can I be inspired by a method while making my own different piece? Yes. A copied picture or invented quotation is unnecessary.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Check a model research record.
Does it name a source and use new wording?
Does the reason point to a feature?
stages.say: Compare A I copied the note and everyone must like this artist with B I explained two facts, named the note and gave my own reason about a feature. Choose B. Rehearse a short private explanation to an adult. The listener asks one factual question; the researcher may say I do not know yet. This supports communication without requiring a peer comment or a public show.
stages.good: The pupil recognises own-word findings, source identification and personal reason as the useful evidence.
stages.fallback: Use the two options orally. The adult can be the listener and the pupil can point to or direct their recorded answer.
stages.answer: If A is chosen, cover the note and help the pupil explain one meaning. Parallel check: Is saying a feature interests me the same as saying everyone must like it? No.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Finish your short research in your arts log.
Name a career fact, a work fact and the source.
Explain one feature and your own next idea.
Share privately, then check the six-row grid.
stages.say: Use about seven minutes to complete the research record in the pupil’s own words, checking any final facts against the chosen source. Add a specific reason the artist interests or inspires the pupil, and one original next idea. If inspiration remains uncertain, record that honestly and identify what they would explore next. Use about two minutes for a private explanation to one adult or a freely chosen listener. Record the actual date, what was shared and one response, or mark sharing pending if the pupil opts out. Use about five minutes to check all six grid rows, reusing Monday’s comments and adding rows 4 to 6. Row 6 points to the actual research. Record help and honest gaps. No new art reproduction or copied text is needed.
stages.good: The final record has one chosen artist, a question, checked career and work facts, source details, a feature-specific personal response, an original idea and actual sharing status. All six outcomes have truthful comments.
stages.fallback: The pupil gives an oral, signed or directed explanation. An adult records exact words and actual sharing, with read-back. If writing materials are absent, record later and keep the transcription pending meanwhile.
stages.answer: Research can support later arts inspiration evidence when it shows genuine enquiry, learning and personal response. A private adult share is a valid classroom route. Any future qualification judgement checks the whole portfolio and current requirements.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Check that the research sounds like you.
Read one fact, one reason and your next idea.
Keep real evidence for each grid row.
stages.say: Use the source note to check facts and the pupil to check personal wording. Read scribed words back. Confirm one next step and any missing evidence. Make no automatic award or full-level claim. Use the final two minutes to store the log and grid together.
stages.good: The pupil recognises their own research and can locate the supporting source and half-term evidence.
stages.fallback: Read short parts aloud and let the pupil confirm, correct or indicate an uncertainty.
stages.answer: An uncompleted share remains pending. A source note in the folder is not by itself the pupil’s research or a completed arts award.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My research is kept in ___.
This feature interests me because ___.
My own next idea is ___.
stages.say: Record the real location of the final research and assessment grid. Keep it in the current Explore log with a clear progression note. The six-week teaching sequence ends here. Identify any evidence gaps for later support without promising certification or filling them in advance.
stages.good: The final research, grid and next step are findable, dated and truthful.
stages.fallback: Retain a precise dated witness record of the pupil’s confirmed words, source and support.
stages.answer: The short record can be retained for later review of arts inspiration evidence. The whole next level includes other work and cannot be awarded from this record alone.
